title: Banda Singh Bahadur
hook: an ascetic from the south meets Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded and becomes the Khalsa's commander

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahankar, and your line, the real battle. That closed our days on sword and saint. Today a long new stretch begins: Sikh history after the Gurus. Day two hundred eighty-two.

Nanded, on the banks of the Godavari river, deep in the south of India, 1708. A holy man lives in a hermitage there. He has left the world behind: no family, no possessions, many followers, and a reputation for strange powers. People say visitors who sit on his special seat get tipped off it. One day he comes home and finds a stranger sitting on that seat, completely at ease. The stranger is Guru Gobind Singh. Today: Banda Singh Bahadur.
screen: `NANDED, ON THE GODAVARI, 1708.` → `A HERMIT WITH A SPECIAL SEAT.` → `A STRANGER SITTING ON IT.`

segments.voice: The hermit's story, as tradition tells it, started far from Nanded. He was born in 1670 in the hills near Kashmir and named Lachhman Dev. As a young man, the story goes, he went hunting and killed a doe, and watched her unborn young die with her. It shook him so badly that he gave up the world and became a wandering ascetic, called Madho Das. He ended up in the south, at Nanded. Guru Gobind Singh had come south too, after losing his sons and his city. Now the two men meet. Tradition says Madho Das tried his powers on the Guru, and they did nothing. Shaken, he asked who this was. And then he said, in effect: I am your banda. Banda means servant, one who is bound to another. He took amrit, and the name that stuck was Banda Singh. Later people added Bahadur, the brave. Here's the turn. The Guru didn't ask Banda to go deeper into his hermitage. He asked him to go out: to Punjab, where the Sikhs were being crushed and the killers of the Guru's young sons still held power. Tradition says the Guru gave him five arrows from his own quiver, a flag, a drum, and a small band of Sikhs, with letters asking the Khalsa to rally behind him. The Guru himself died at Nanded later that year. So the man who'd walked away from the world was sent straight back into it. For Sikhs, Banda's story is a picture of what a call can do. Sometimes the service asked of you is the thing you'd left behind.
screen: `LACHHMAN DEV, THEN MADHO DAS.` · `A HERMIT AT NANDED.` · `BANDA — THE GURU'S SERVANT.` · `SENT BACK OUT TO PUNJAB.` · then, large: `CALLED TO SERVE.`

segments.voice: Think of a direction you've been walking in for a while. A habit, a job, a way of spending evenings, a way of treating someone. Ask it honestly: is this where I'm needed? Picture a small change of direction, just one degree, toward someone who could use you. A call you've been avoiding, a skill you've kept to yourself. Hold that picture. You don't have to act yet. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Banda. A servant, one bound to another — the name the hermit Madho Das took when he pledged himself to Guru Gobind Singh and was sent to lead the Khalsa.
Your line: called to serve. Today, change direction once, toward someone who could use your help. Day two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur as the commander Guru Gobind Singh sent to lead the Khalsa in Punjab; the gurdwara at Nanded, Hazur Sahib, is one of the five takhts, marking where Guru Gobind Singh spent his last days.

original.note: Gurmukhi: banda, a servant, one bound to another; bahadur means brave.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh general's name.
what it means: a hermit who called himself the Guru's servant and was sent back into the world to serve.

what a scholar hears: born Lachhman Dev (1670), ascetic name Madho Das; the meeting at Nanded in 1708 comes from traditional accounts, which differ on details such as the arrows and the size of his band.

sources.ref: The meeting of Guru Gobind Singh and Madho Das at Nanded, 1708, as told in Sikh tradition

notes: Birth year 1670 and birthplace near Rajouri (Jammu and Kashmir) are standard but based on traditional accounts; confirm.
The doe story and the seat story are traditional; framed as 'tradition says'.
Whether Banda formally took amrit and the name Gurbakhsh Singh is debated; the script says he 'took amrit'. Keeper to confirm.
The outline hook says 'an ascetic from the south'; the script clarifies he was born in the north and settled in the south.
Review (fresh editor): howItsDone no longer calls Banda the Khalsa's 'first' commander (unsourced superlative); otherwise left as written.
